To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) stress changes applied on stable interfaces trigger localized creep episodes; (ii) stress transfer due to creeping segments strongly influences the timing of seismic ruptures on adjacent unstable interfaces; and (iii) stress changes trigger aftershock sequences whose rate decays much faster than  1/time shortly after an earthquake.

the nucleation patch of a rupture on a rate‐ and state ‐dependent frictional interface is not a constant size, but depends on the stressing history, and that the interaction of a creeping segment with a seismic segment may trigger aftershocks, but the aftershock sequence is not necessarily a simple power law.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interaction of seismic and creep processes on rate‐ and‐state‐dependent faults.
the interaction between the creep on intraslab faults and the seismicity on the faults in the vicinity.
the effect of creep on the nucleation of earthquakes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
stress changes on intrinsically unstable faults can trigger aftershocks, but stress changes on intrisically stable faults cannot trigger seismic slip.

the interaction between creep on stable faults and seismic slip on unstable faults is a very complex process, and the details of the interaction depend on the constitutive laws of the faults, their geometrical arrangement, and the loading history.
the nucleation process is a complex process, and that the interaction between the nucleation process and the surrounding medium can have a strong effect on the evolution of the nucleation process.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the interaction between the seismic and creeping segments of a fault is very complex and can be understood only by considering the details of the constitutive law.

, in addition to the classical nucleation of seismic ruptures on unstable faults, we have shown that the nucleation of quasi‐static slip on intrinsically creep‐prone faults, as well as the interaction between creep‐prone and seismic faults, are also nucleation processes.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the nucleation of quasi-static slip on intrinsically rate‐ and state ‐ dependent faults is a complex process, and that the interaction of seismic faults with creep can strongly modify the seismicity of the system. [2]
